12.0.big: Gregor Mendel worked out the basic rules of inheritance by carefully breeding thousands of pea plants and counting the results.
points: We now know Mendel's "factors" are genes on chromosomes.
Not every gene follows Mendel's simple rules, but they're the starting point for all of genetics.

12.1.big: Mendel crossed true-breeding pea plants and found that traits don't blend. One trait hides in the first generation (F1) and comes back in a 3:1 ratio in the next (F2).
points: Peas were perfect: they normally self-pollinate (so they breed true), grow in one season, and you can grow thousands of them.
P0 (parents) → F1 (their kids) → F2 (grandkids). F1 all showed the dominant trait, and the recessive trait came back in about ¼ of F2.
This disproved the blending theory: the recessive trait was hidden, not lost.
Product rule ("and"): multiply. The chance of event A and event B is P(A) × P(B).
Sum rule ("or"): add. The chance of A or B (when they can't both happen) is P(A) + P(B).
Big samples matter. Small ones can stray from the expected ratio just by chance.
12.1.tip: "And" means multiply; "or" means add. Example: chance of two heads in a row = ½ × ½ = ¼.

12.2.big: Your genotype is which alleles you carry, like Yy. Your phenotype is what shows, like yellow. A Punnett square predicts what offspring will get.
points: Homozygous: two of the same allele (YY or yy). Heterozygous: two different (Yy). A recessive trait shows only when homozygous (yy).
Yy × Yy gives a genotype ratio of 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy, and a phenotype ratio of 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

Test cross: cross a dominant-looking individual with a recessive one (yy). If all the offspring show the dominant trait, the parent is probably YY. If about half show the recessive trait, the parent is Yy.
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between (red × white snapdragons → pink).
Codominance: both alleles show fully (AB blood type, MN blood groups).
Multiple alleles: a population can have more than two versions of a gene (ABO blood types, rabbit coat colors).
X-linked traits: males have one X, so one recessive allele is enough. That's why color blindness and hemophilia are far more common in males.
Lethal alleles: a recessive lethal kills homozygotes, so Aa × Aa gives a 2:1 ratio among survivors.

12.3.big: Mendel's laws: each parent passes on one of their two alleles (segregation), and genes on different chromosomes sort independently. Linked genes and gene interactions are the exceptions.
points: Law of segregation: the two alleles separate when gametes form (homologs separate in anaphase I), so each gamete gets one.
Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes don't affect each other's sorting (homologous pairs line up randomly in metaphase I).
Dihybrid cross (YyRr × YyRr): a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio, which is just two 3:1 ratios multiplied together.

For lots of genes, use the forked-line or probability method instead of a giant Punnett square. With n heterozygous genes you get 2<sup>n</sup> gamete types, 3<sup>n</sup> genotypes and 2<sup>n</sup> phenotypes.
Linkage: genes close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, unless crossing over separates them.
Epistasis: one gene masks another. In mice, cc means albino no matter what the A gene says, giving a 9:3:4 ratio.
12.3.tip: Any ratio that adds up to 16 (9:3:3:1, 9:3:4, 12:3:1, 15:1) means two genes are involved.

stem: What conclusions about the physical relationship between the traits can be drawn from the experiment?
opts: The traits are probably coded by linked genes.
The traits follow the law of independent assortment.
The traits are located on different chromosomes.

1.why: Pollen comes from the anther, the male part. Mendel moved it onto the stigma of another plant.

2.why: Seed texture (round or wrinkled) was one of Mendel's seven characteristics.

3.why: True-breeding YY × yy gives all Yy, so 100% yellow: the dominant trait.

4.why: The F2 ratio is 3 inflated : 1 constricted, and 650 ÷ 3 ≈ 217.

5.why: The traits you can observe make up the phenotype.

6.why: A recessive trait shows only when someone has two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous).

7.why: Gray is a blend between black and white, which means incomplete dominance.

8.why: There are three alleles (multiple alleles), and A and B are both fully expressed in AB (codominance).

9.why: Normally 1:2:1, but the homozygous recessive offspring die before birth, so it's 1 : 2 : 0.

10.why: Both methods multiply the chances for each gene: the product rule.

11.why: s from one parent and s from the other gives ss.

12.why: Genes on separate chromosomes assort independently, just as Mendel's laws describe.

13.why: With 3 heterozygous genes: 33 = 27 genotypes and 23 = 8 phenotypes.

14.why: RR × rr can only give Rr, and Rr is pink (incomplete dominance).

15.why: Homologous pairs line up randomly in meiosis I, so genes on different chromosomes sort independently.

16.why: Each gamete gets one of each pair, which is the law of segregation.

17.why: One gene hiding the effect of another is epistasis.

18.why: Independent assortment would give 9:3:3:1. Instead, the parental combinations (purple/long and white/round) dominate and only a few recombinants appear, so the genes are linked on the same chromosome.

19.why: One gene masking or changing another's effect is epistasis.

20.why: Pea flowers stay tightly closed, which prevents cross-fertilization, so plants self-pollinate and breed true. That gave Mendel control over every cross.

21.why: A reciprocal cross swaps which parent gives the pollen: true-breeding tall pollen on a dwarf plant, then dwarf pollen on a tall plant.

22.why: AA × aa gives all Aa (axial) in F1. Aa × Aa then gives AA (axial), Aa (axial) and aa (terminal) in F2.

23.why: tt × Tt gives ½ Tt (tall) and ½ tt (dwarf), so 1 : 1.

24.why: Color blindness is X-linked. Males have only one X, so one recessive allele means they have the condition. They can't be hidden carriers.

25.why: AA × Aa → ½ AA, ½ Aa. BB × bb → all Bb. Cc × cc → ½ Cc, ½ cc. Combined: AABbCc, AABbcc, AaBbCc and AaBbcc, each ¼, so 1:1:1:1.

26.why: Pairs line up randomly in metaphase I, homologs separate in anaphase I, and sister chromatids separate in anaphase II, giving four different haploid gametes.

27.why: Any dominant W makes the fruit white (W is epistatic to Y). With ww, Y_ gives yellow, and only wwyy is green.

28.why: The father's mother had a straight hairline (ww), so the father must be Ww. Ww × ww gives ½ widow's peak, so 0.5.

29.why: The weak taster is a heterozygote and the strong taster is homozygous. The father passes on a tasting allele every time, so the son can't be a non-taster: 0.

30.why: Knowing they're both carriers gives them medical information: each child has a ¼ chance of Tay-Sachs, so they can plan and get tested.

31.why: Every birth is independent. Earlier children don't matter, so it's still 50%.

32.why: Daughter and daughter and daughter: ½ × ½ × ½ = ⅛.

33.why: Blue × red gives violet, an in-between color, which is incomplete dominance.

34.why: Violet × violet (both heterozygous) gives 1 blue : 2 violet : 1 red, so 25% / 50% / 25%.

35.why: The F1 all looked wild type, so gray body and red eyes are dominant.

36.why: Predicting equal numbers of all four combinations assumes the traits assort independently. Big differences from that prediction point to linkage.

37.why: Calico shows both colors at once (codominance), and the gene is on the X chromosome (sex-linked).

38.why: Since it's X-linked, the outcome depends on which parent is male. Daughters would be calico, but sons get their color from the mother. We aren't told which cat is which, so there isn't enough information.
